paragraphs: Distributed training requires machines to exchange information about gradients, and compressing that information can reduce communication. This paper introduces three point compressors, or 3PC, together with distributed algorithms for nonconvex optimization. Its central design choice is to let the compressor change during training instead of committing to a fixed compression rule throughout the process.

The framework brings existing and new methods into one mathematical treatment. It recovers the EF21 error feedback mechanism and its theoretical properties as a special case, while also producing additional efficient algorithms. This connection matters because the proposed class extends an established approach while retaining a route to understanding its guarantees.

The authors also report improvements to the algorithms and theory of lazy aggregation, and establish a connection between lazy aggregation and error feedback. Their analysis does not require compressors to be unbiased. Together, these contributions broaden the compression mechanisms available for communication-efficient training and provide a shared foundation for methods previously studied in separate lines of work.
icml-2022-3pc-three-point-compressors-fo.tldr: 3PC lets gradient compressors evolve during distributed training, unifying error feedback and lazy aggregation while enabling new communication-efficient methods.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods assign importance to parts of an input, but judging those assignments is itself difficult. In image tasks, popular evaluations perturb pixels and examine the consequences. Different versions of these evaluations can disagree about which attribution method is best, and some require expensive model retraining.

This paper analyzes pixel-perturbation evaluations using information theory. It identifies a confounding signal: the shape formed by the removed pixels can leak information, independently of the pixel values being assessed. Consequently, an evaluation may partly measure information conveyed by the removal pattern, weakening its ability to isolate the quality of the attribution.

The proposed Remove and Debias framework, ROAD, uses this analysis to reduce the influence of those confounders. The authors report greater consistency across evaluation strategies and computational savings of up to 99% relative to the state of the art, because ROAD avoids retraining. The contribution therefore concerns both the credibility of attribution comparisons and the practical cost of carrying them out.
icml-2022-a-consistent-and-efficient-eva.tldr: ROAD makes attribution evaluations more consistent and cheaper by reducing information leakage from pixel-removal patterns and avoiding retraining.

paragraphs: Meta-learning uses experience from related tasks to learn an inductive bias, including hyperparameters for the learning algorithm applied within each task. A central question is how well that learned bias transfers beyond the observed data. This paper studies that question through PAC-Bayes bounds on the meta-generalization gap.

The analysis separates two sources of uncertainty. Observing only a finite number of tasks creates an environment-level gap, while observing only a finite number of examples within each task creates a task-level gap. The authors derive new bounds by upper bounding convex functions that connect empirical losses with expected losses at both levels. This provides a common mathematical route for handling the two gaps together.

The bounds also serve as the basis for new meta-learning algorithms, connecting the theoretical analysis to a training procedure. Numerical examples demonstrate advantages over earlier PAC-Bayes bounds and algorithms for meta-learning. These findings support the usefulness of the proposed formulation in the examined examples, alongside its contribution to understanding how limited task and sample counts affect generalization.
icml-2022-a-unified-view-on-pac-bayes-bo.tldr: A unified PAC-Bayes analysis accounts for limited tasks and limited examples per task, yielding new meta-learning bounds and algorithms.

paragraphs: Point cloud classification assigns categories to objects represented by collections of points in three-dimensional space. Although classification performance has advanced, deployed systems encounter corrupted inputs caused by complex scenes, inaccurate sensors, and imperfect processing. This paper asks how well representative point cloud models withstand those disruptions.

The authors first organize common three-dimensional corruptions into a taxonomy and identify atomic corruption types. They then use this structure to evaluate a broad range of models systematically. The taxonomy gives the investigation a consistent basis for comparing robustness and generalizability, rather than treating each corruption as an unrelated test case.

The benchmark suggests that improving classification performance over time has not brought matching gains in robustness: leading methods appear close to becoming less robust. Drawing on patterns in the evaluation, the authors propose several techniques that improve classifier robustness. The work makes corruption resilience an explicit dimension of progress in three-dimensional perception and supplies both an assessment framework and practical directions for improving it.
icml-2022-benchmarking-and-analyzing-poi.tldr: A systematic corruption benchmark finds that advances in point cloud classification do not necessarily bring stronger robustness and proposes techniques to improve it.

paragraphs: Most neural simulators predict a future physical state directly from the current state. This paper instead learns a constraint function and obtains the next state by solving an optimization problem defined by that function. The approach draws on traditional simulation engines, which construct states by satisfying constraints.

A graph neural network implements the scalar constraint function. Separating the learned description of the system from the procedure used to find its next state creates useful flexibility at inference time. The authors show that applying more solver iterations can improve accuracy when simulating a larger system, allowing additional computation to refine the prediction.

The framework also accepts new hand-designed constraints at test time, enabling simulations of dynamics absent from the training data. Across a variety of challenging physical domains, it achieves accuracy comparable to or better than leading learned simulators. These results show how constraint solving can provide a useful inductive bias while making a learned simulator adaptable through both its solver and its constraints.
icml-2022-constraint-based-graph-network.tldr: A graph network learns physical constraints, letting an optimization solver produce accurate simulations and incorporate new constraints at test time.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to learn from a sequence of data or tasks while retaining useful predictive knowledge. Sequential Bayesian inference offers a natural way to update that knowledge, but applying it to neural networks has been difficult. This paper develops an objective by treating continual learning as sequential variational inference over predictive functions.

Working in function space changes what the training objective constrains. Rather than directly restricting neural network parameters, it allows those parameters to move substantially, supporting adaptation to new tasks. Compared with approaches that directly regularize predictions, the proposed formulation also permits more flexible variational distributions and provides more effective regularization.

Across the task sequences examined, networks trained with this objective achieve higher predictive accuracy than related methods. They also rely less on retaining representative points from earlier tasks. The findings suggest that preserving knowledge through a distribution over functions can support adaptation without tying it as tightly to particular parameter values or to a maintained collection of past examples.
icml-2022-continual-learning-via-sequent.tldr: Sequential inference over predictive functions improves continual-learning accuracy while allowing parameter flexibility and reducing reliance on representative past examples.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning commonly expresses desired behavior through a reward function. Specifying acceptable and forbidden actions this way can require repeated manual adjustments, and an agent may exploit the reward without behaving as intended. This paper investigates whether explicit behavioral constraints can make that specification process more practical.

The authors formulate behavioral preferences using constrained Markov decision processes. Lagrangian methods automatically assign weights to the constraints, addressing a part of the process that otherwise falls to manual reward engineering. The work specifically examines goal-based tasks in which the agent must pursue an objective while respecting several constraints simultaneously.

The framework is evaluated on continuous-control tasks relevant to designing non-player characters in video games. Its broader proposal is to use constrained reinforcement learning beyond its usual safety-focused role, as a tool for expressing behavioral requirements. The abstract presents reduced reward-specification effort as a potential benefit; the central contribution is a framework for making those requirements explicit and learning their relative weighting.
icml-2022-direct-behavior-specification-.tldr: The paper uses explicit behavioral constraints and automatic Lagrangian weighting to make goal-directed reinforcement learning easier to specify.

paragraphs: Medical image models need explanations that make their predictions understandable, yet popular explanation methods can produce incomplete or noisy results in this setting. This paper focuses on attention weights, which describe the input regions emphasized by a model. It asks how attention across multiple convolutional layers can provide consistent interpretations.

The proposed mechanism uses convex optimization to enforce consistency between the attended layers. The authors apply duality to separate the constraints between layers by reparameterizing their attention probability distributions. They then learn the dual witness through the training objective, allowing the implementation to use standard backpropagation efficiently.

The method uses weakly annotated medical images and preserves predictive performance while providing explanations the authors describe as complete and faithful to the model's prediction. Its contribution links explanation quality to an explicit relationship among layers: attention is trained to remain consistent across the network. This provides a way to integrate interpretability requirements into the model rather than relying solely on a separate explanation procedure.
icml-2022-dual-decomposition-of-convex-o.tldr: Convex consistency constraints align attention across medical-image network layers, producing faithful explanations while preserving predictive performance.

paragraphs: A networked dynamical system has both a connection structure and local rules governing how its nodes change state. Earlier active-query approaches often assumed the connections were already known and learned only the local rules. This paper studies how to infer both pieces together by choosing queries to the system.

The authors consider two ways to organize those queries. In the batch model, all queries must be submitted together. In the adaptive model, responses to earlier queries can guide subsequent ones. Their results apply to systems with binary node states and Boolean local functions, and cover several classes within that setting.

For both query models, the paper presents algorithms that learn the network topology and its behavior using a polynomial number of queries. It also reports experiments with query-generation algorithms on synthetic and real-world networks. The contribution shows that unknown connections need not prevent efficient identification for the studied system classes, while distinguishing what can be achieved with and without feedback during query selection.
icml-2022-efficiently-learning-the-topol.tldr: Active-query algorithms learn both connections and local rules for several classes of binary dynamical systems using polynomially many queries.

paragraphs: Instrumental variable methods can identify a causal relationship even when unobserved factors confound the observed inputs and response. Many estimators require instruments to be uncorrelated with response errors and hidden confounders. This paper examines the stronger restriction of independence, which can be justified by the same graphical separation arguments often used to motivate the weaker condition.

The authors show that exploiting independence yields strictly stronger identifiability results. They introduce HSIC-X, a practical method compatible with any gradient-based learning procedure. Accounting for higher moments may also improve results with finite data, even when the causal function is already identifiable under the existing setup.

Independence further supports generalization when the distribution of the instruments changes. The proposed estimator is proved invariant to shifts on the instruments and worst-case optimal when those shifts are sufficiently strong. These results also cover under-identified settings, where the instruments cannot fully determine the causal function. Thus, the paper distinguishes identifying causality from achieving robustness to a specified family of distribution changes.
icml-2022-exploiting-independent-instrum.tldr: HSIC-X exploits instrument independence to strengthen causal identification and obtain guarantees against distribution shifts affecting the instruments.

paragraphs: Newton-type optimization uses Hessians to describe curvature, but communicating this information creates challenges in federated learning. FedNL addresses them with a family of methods that learn local Hessian information efficiently. Its Hessian-learning procedure does not require revealing training data to the coordinating server and applies beyond generalized linear models.

The method supports general contractive compression operators, including Top-K and Rank-R, without requiring error feedback. Additional variants support partial participation, cubic regularization, line search, and compression in both communication directions. These extensions address distinct practical requirements: not every participant must contribute each time, and information sent to and from the server can be compressed.

The authors prove local convergence rates independent of the condition number, training-data count, and compression variance. They also prove that the Hessian-learning procedure learns the Hessian at the optimum. Numerical experiments report state-of-the-art communication complexity against key baselines. Together, these results advance the use of curvature information in federated optimization, with the convergence-rate claim specifically applying locally.
icml-2022-fednl-making-newton-type-metho.tldr: FedNL learns compressed Hessians to make Newton-type federated optimization more communication-efficient, with local convergence guarantees and practical participation variants.

paragraphs: Implicit processes offer a flexible way to describe models, including Bayesian neural networks and data generators, and to perform approximate inference over functions. Working with functions addresses difficulties caused by the large number of parameters and strong parameter dependencies in large models. However, obtaining a suitably flexible inference method remains challenging.

The paper identifies a split in existing approaches. Methods that can adjust the prior implicit process to the data produce Gaussian predictive distributions, which can miss important patterns. Methods that use an implicit process for a more flexible posterior distribution cannot tune the prior to the observations. Each approach therefore achieves only one of these two objectives.

The proposed method combines both capabilities through an inducing-point representation of the prior, drawing on an approach used in sparse Gaussian processes. The resulting approximate inference procedure is scalable, learns prior parameters from the data, and produces accurate non-Gaussian predictive distributions. Its contribution is to make prior adaptation and predictive flexibility available within the same implicit-process framework.
icml-2022-function-space-inference-with-.tldr: Sparse implicit processes combine data-adapted priors with flexible non-Gaussian predictions in a scalable function-space inference method.

paragraphs: GraphCON builds graph neural networks from the dynamics of coupled oscillators. Its starting point is a second-order differential equation describing nonlinear oscillators with control and damping, connected according to the graph. Discretizing those dynamics produces a multilayer neural network, with a basic graph-network layer supplying the coupling function.

This construction accommodates different coupling choices, including convolutional and attention-based layers. The authors connect oversmoothing, where graph representations become excessively alike, to the stability of steady states in the differential equation. They show that steady states with zero Dirichlet energy are unstable in their proposed dynamics, establishing that the framework mitigates oversmoothing.

The paper also proves that GraphCON mitigates exploding and vanishing gradients, helping train deeper graph networks. Experiments show competitive performance against leading methods across several graph-learning tasks. The framework therefore offers both an architectural recipe and a dynamical explanation for its behavior: properties of the underlying equations help address difficulties that arise as graph networks become deeper.
icml-2022-graph-coupled-oscillator-netwo.tldr: GraphCON builds graph networks from coupled-oscillator dynamics that mitigate oversmoothing and unstable gradients while achieving competitive performance.

paragraphs: LINAC transforms images using implicit neural representations that approximately encode pixel colors. Classifiers trained on these transformed images appear resistant to small adversarial perturbations without adversarial training or large performance drops. On CIFAR-10, the defense hinders several common attacks at perturbation sizes up to 8/255 in the Linf norm and 0.5 in the L2 norm.

The random seed used to initialize and train the image representation emerges as necessary information for stronger generic attacks. The authors therefore suggest that it plays a role resembling a private key. To investigate this type of defense, they develop the Parametric Bypass Approximation attack, which successfully invalidates an existing key-based method.

LINAC also hinders some transfer and adaptive attacks, including the new bypass strategy. These findings remain specific to the attacks examined: the paper emphasizes that apparent robustness in standard evaluations calls for broader, customized testing. Its contribution combines a defensive input transformation with an attack method that helps probe whether key-dependent defenses withstand more targeted evaluation.
icml-2022-hindering-adversarial-attacks-.tldr: LINAC hinders several tested adversarial attacks through image re-encoding, while a new bypass attack highlights the need for customized robustness evaluations.

paragraphs: In a network game, each player's payoff depends on their own action and the actions of neighboring players. Observed equilibrium actions therefore contain information about the underlying connections. Recovering those connections could help analyze economic and social interactions, but existing methods usually require knowledge of the utility function governing the game.

This paper learns a mapping from equilibrium actions to network structure without explicitly knowing that utility function. It uses a transformer-like architecture designed to account correctly for the symmetries of the inference problem. The architectural design makes those symmetries part of the method for interpreting observed actions and reconstructing the network.

The authors evaluate the method on three types of network games using synthetic and real-world data. They report effective structure recovery and better performance than existing methods in those evaluations. The work shows a way to infer strategic relationships when explicit utility information is unavailable, replacing that requirement with a learned mapping whose architecture reflects the structure of the problem.
icml-2022-learning-to-infer-structures-o.tldr: A symmetry-aware, transformer-like model infers network-game connections from equilibrium actions without explicit knowledge of the utility function.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations make predictions through evolving dynamics. LyaNet trains those dynamics using a stability condition from control theory. Its Lyapunov loss encourages the inference trajectory to move quickly toward the correct prediction, making the behavior of the trajectory an explicit target of learning.

The authors prove that minimizing this loss guarantees exponential convergence to the correct solution and enables a robustness guarantee. Exponential convergence describes how quickly the dynamics approach the solution, so the theoretical result concerns the process of reaching a prediction as well as its destination. The paper also gives practical training algorithms, including one that avoids backpropagating through a differential-equation solver or using the adjoint method.

Compared with standard Neural ODE training, experiments find that LyaNet can improve predictive performance, accelerate convergence during inference, and increase adversarial robustness. These are reported empirical possibilities rather than universal improvements. The contribution connects a control-theoretic training objective, formal convergence behavior, and practical methods for learning the dynamics.
icml-2022-lyanet-a-lyapunov-framework-fo.tldr: LyaNet trains Neural ODEs with a Lyapunov loss that guarantees exponential convergence when minimized and can improve prediction, inference speed, and robustness.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using historical logs rather than deploying it. In contextual bandits, commonly used estimators rely on inverse propensity weighting. When there are many possible actions, these estimators can suffer severe bias and variance, making offline policy comparisons unreliable.

The proposed estimator uses action embeddings to exploit structure among the available actions. It replaces conventional importance weights with marginalized importance weights. The authors analyze the resulting bias, variance, and mean squared error, and identify conditions under which the embedding provides statistical advantages over conventional estimators. The benefit therefore depends on how the embedding supports the evaluation problem.

Experiments show that the improvement can be substantial, with reliable evaluation in large-action settings where existing estimators break down. The contribution connects a representation of actions to the statistical properties of policy evaluation. This matters for applications with many choices, such as recommendation and language modeling, where collecting logs alone does not ensure that a new policy can be evaluated accurately.
icml-2022-off-policy-evaluation-for-larg.tldr: An embedding-based estimator can make offline policy evaluation more reliable in large action spaces by using marginalized importance weights.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn from pairwise comparisons: at each round, an agent selects two items and receives only a binary win-or-loss outcome. This paper studies environments where the underlying preferences change over time. Dynamic regret evaluates the learner against a changing comparison benchmark, making it relevant when a single fixed choice cannot represent good performance throughout.

The authors first develop an efficient algorithm with static regret of order square root of KT for adversarial preferences. They then give dynamic-regret guarantees for two kinds of change: effective switches and continuous variation. The respective rates are square root of SKT and V_T to the one-third power times K to the one-third power times T to the two-thirds power, up to logarithmic factors.

Matching lower bounds establish optimality of the stated dynamic-regret rates. The algorithms can also be reused to obtain guarantees for Condorcet, best-response, and Borda notions of regret. Simulations support the results, which connect achievable learning performance to both the number of choices and the amount of preference change.
icml-2022-optimal-and-efficient-dynamic-.tldr: Efficient dueling-bandit algorithms achieve provably optimal dynamic-regret rates for switching and continuously varying preferences.

paragraphs: Quantization-aware training prepares models to operate with low-precision values. Clipping helps control quantization noise, but common methods choose clipping thresholds heuristically. This paper introduces OCTAV, a recursive algorithm that selects clipping scalars to minimize mean squared quantization error, giving the threshold choice a defined optimization objective.

Derived from Newton-Raphson iteration, OCTAV updates the clipping scalar for each tensor at every training iteration. This yields provably minimum quantization noise at each step under the stated mean squared error objective. The authors also identify shortcomings in common gradient estimators for quantization-aware training and introduce magnitude-aware differentiation to improve accuracy further.

Experiments report state-of-the-art accuracy across training and retraining ResNets and MobileNets on ImageNet and fine-tuning BERT on Squad. OCTAV-enabled training consistently preserves accuracy at four-to-six-bit precision in these evaluations. The results use the baseline training recipes with quantization operations inserted where appropriate. The work therefore combines principled threshold selection with an improved differentiation method while keeping the surrounding training procedure intact.
icml-2022-optimal-clipping-and-magnitude.tldr: OCTAV minimizes clipping-related quantization error during training, while magnitude-aware differentiation helps preserve accuracy at four-to-six-bit precision.

paragraphs: Minimizing average prediction loss can produce accurate models that remain vulnerable to input perturbations. Adversarial training addresses this by training against worst-case perturbations, but that objective can be overly conservative and reduce nominal performance. This paper proposes probabilistic robustness as an intermediate goal: robustness to most perturbations rather than every perturbation.

The framework changes the robustness requirement itself, allowing the learning objective to occupy a position between average-case and worst-case performance. The authors provide theoretical results overcoming performance and sample-complexity trade-offs associated with those two extremes. The distinction matters because a probabilistic robustness requirement does not claim protection against all possible perturbations.

For practical training, the paper introduces a risk-aware optimization algorithm that balances average and worst-case performance at considerably lower computational cost than adversarial training. Results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN illustrate advantages across that spectrum. Together, the framework and algorithm offer a way to select a less conservative robustness target while still explicitly accounting for perturbation risk.
icml-2022-probabilistically-robust-learn.tldr: Probabilistic robustness targets most perturbations, balancing ordinary accuracy and robustness with lower training cost than adversarial training.

paragraphs: Combining Monte Carlo sampling with deep learning offers a way to solve partial differential equations in high dimensions. Some approaches turn the equation into a loss-minimization problem using an associated stochastic differential equation. Their practical success then depends on whether the gradients used for training can be estimated accurately and with low variance.

This paper investigates those numerical issues for linear Kolmogorov equations. The authors systematically compare existing deep-learning approaches and explain their performance theoretically. Their focus connects the mathematical formulation of the loss with the numerical behavior of the optimization procedure, particularly the quality of the gradient estimates it produces.

Building on that analysis, they propose new methods that are more robust both in theory and in numerical evaluations, with substantial reported performance improvements. The work shows why the formulation of a learning problem matters even when the ultimate goal is the same differential-equation solution. Improving how the objective is estimated and optimized can help the solver converge more accurately and quickly.
icml-2022-robust-sde-based-variational-f.tldr: The paper analyzes gradient-estimation issues in neural solvers for linear Kolmogorov PDEs and develops theoretically and numerically more robust formulations.

paragraphs: Causal discovery seeks to recover the directed relationships among variables from data. This paper shows how information in the score of a data distribution can support that recovery. Its setting is nonlinear additive-noise models with Gaussian noise, so the proposed connection is established within a specified class of causal models.

The approach uses score-matching algorithms as a building block for scalable causal discovery. It also introduces an efficient way to approximate the score's Jacobian, which describes how the score changes across variables. That approximation enables recovery of the causal graph and turns the conceptual connection between distributional information and causal structure into an algorithm called SCORE.

Empirical comparisons find SCORE competitive with state-of-the-art causal-discovery methods while being significantly faster. The finding supports its value as an efficient graph-recovery method in the evaluated settings. More broadly, the paper provides a route for constructing causal-discovery algorithms around score estimation, with the nonlinear additive Gaussian-noise assumption defining the scope of the stated recovery result.
icml-2022-score-matching-enables-causal-.tldr: SCORE uses score matching and an efficient Jacobian approximation to recover causal graphs in nonlinear additive Gaussian-noise models.

paragraphs: Short-term plasticity stores fading memories in synapses. This paper turns that mechanism into a recurrent neural unit called the STP Neuron, or STPN. Each synapse carries a state that evolves through its own recurrent connection, allowing the connection itself to hold changing information over time.

The formulation makes plasticity trainable through backpropagation through time. The network can therefore learn how to retain and forget information over short periods. Across the reported tests, STPN outperforms all tested alternatives, including RNNs, LSTMs, other fast-weight models, and differentiable-plasticity models. The evaluations span supervised and reinforcement learning, including associative retrieval, maze exploration, Atari games, and MuJoCo robotics.

The authors also calculate that STPN minimizes energy use among the compared models in neuromorphic or biological circuits because it dynamically depresses individual synapses. They suggest that biological short-term plasticity may consequently offer an evolutionary advantage in efficiency and computational power. That biological interpretation is a possibility, while the machine-learning results establish the unit's performance across the tested tasks.
icml-2022-short-term-plasticity-neurons-.tldr: STP Neurons learn short-term synaptic memory and forgetting, outperforming tested recurrent alternatives and offering calculated energy advantages in neuromorphic or biological circuits.

paragraphs: Attention mechanisms perform well in vision tasks, but the preferences they build into a model are less well understood. This paper uses convex duality to examine those inductive biases. It analyzes nonlinear dot-product self-attention alongside alternative mechanisms, including MLP-mixer and the Fourier Neural Operator.

The authors derive equivalent finite-dimensional convex optimization problems that can be interpreted and solved to global optimality. These formulations reveal block nuclear-norm regularization, which encourages low-rank structure in latent feature and token dimensions. The analysis also shows that self-attention implicitly groups tokens according to their similarity in the latent representation, giving a concrete interpretation of its bias.

To examine the practical value of this perspective, the paper fine-tunes several convex attention heads on a pretrained transformer backbone for CIFAR-100 classification. The results support the advantages of the bias induced by attention compared with existing MLP and linear heads. The contribution connects interpretable optimization structure to a specific transfer-learning evaluation, rather than treating attention's empirical success as an unexplained architectural property.
icml-2022-unraveling-attention-via-conve.tldr: Convex formulations reveal how attention encourages low-rank structure and groups similar tokens, with supporting results from transformer-head fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn by repeatedly asking which of two choices is preferred. This paper studies both stochastic preferences and adversarial preferences, seeking a single method with strong guarantees in either environment. Its central tool is a reduction that translates general dueling-bandit problems into multi-armed-bandit problems.

The reduction yields a best-of-both-worlds algorithm with optimal guarantees for both settings. Against the Condorcet-winner benchmark, it achieves regret of order the sum of log T divided by each arm's suboptimality gap. This captures how difficulty depends on the individual choices, and matching lower bounds establish optimality up to small constant factors.

The authors also prove an optimal regret rate when preferences are adversarially corrupted, improving on previous guarantees for that setting. Empirical comparisons support the algorithms' effectiveness against existing dueling-bandit methods. Beyond these particular results, the reduction offers a common way to approach problems that have often been studied separately, making established multi-armed-bandit techniques useful for learning from relative rather than direct feedback.
icml-2022-versatile-dueling-bandits-best.tldr: A reduction to multi-armed bandits yields optimal dueling-bandit guarantees across stochastic, adversarial, and adversarially corrupted preference settings.
